Hammedatha
ham-mē-dä'thä
n. (the Agagite, father of Haman the enemy of the Jews, named in every formal mention of his son)
A Persian name taken into Hebrew as Hammedatha, generally explained as given by the moon or double. The Authorized Version attaches the Agagite to the family, marking descent from the royal house of Amalek and so setting the whole book of Esther inside an ancient quarrel.

Biblical Definition

Hammedatha is named five times in Esther and never apart from his son. The formula is heavy and deliberate: “did king Ahasuerus promote Haman the son of Hammedatha the Agagite, and advanced him, and set his seat above all the princes that were with him” (Est 3:1); “the king took his ring from his hand, and gave it unto Haman the son of Hammedatha the Agagite, the Jews&#39; enemy” (Est 3:10); Esther pleads to reverse “the letters devised by Haman the son of Hammedatha the Agagite” (Est 8:5); and the record of the deliverance recites it once more: “Because Haman the son of Hammedatha, the Agagite, the enemy of all the Jews, had devised against the Jews to destroy them, and had cast Pur, that is, the lot, to consume them” (Est 9:24). The point of the repetition is the second title, not the first. Agagite reaches back to Agag king of Amalek, whom Saul spared in disobedience and Samuel hewed in pieces before the LORD in Gilgal (1Sa 15:33), and behind Agag to the LORD's oath of perpetual war with Amalek for waylaying Israel in the wilderness. Mordecai is a Benjamite of the house of Kish — Saul's house. The gallows Haman built for the Jew, and the ten sons of Hammedatha's son who hung on it, close a war Saul left unfinished five hundred years earlier.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) has no article for Hammedatha; in sacred history he is the Agagite, father of Haman the enemy of the Jews in the book of Esther.

expand to see more

HAMMEDATHA, n. A Persian proper name in the book of Esther.

The father of Haman, who was advanced above all the princes of Ahasuerus.

He is styled the Agagite, of the royal stock of Amalek.

His son cast Pur, that is, the lot, to determine the day for destroying the Jews.

The ten sons of Haman the son of Hammedatha were slain and hanged in Shushan.

Key Scripture

Est 3:1 — "After these things did king Ahasuerus promote Haman the son of Hammedatha the Agagite, and advanced him, and set his seat above all the princes that were with him."

Est 3:10 — "And the king took his ring from his hand, and gave it unto Haman the son of Hammedatha the Agagite, the Jews' enemy."

Est 9:10 — "The ten sons of Haman the son of Hammedatha, the enemy of the Jews, slew they; but on the spoil laid they not their hand."

Est 9:24 — "Because Haman the son of Hammedatha, the Agagite, the enemy of all the Jews, had devised against the Jews to destroy them, and had cast Pur, that is, the lot, to consume them, and to destroy them;"

Modern Corruption

Esther is widely read as a secular court tale in which God does not appear and the Jews merely outmanoeuvre their enemies. The genealogy Scripture insists on — Agagite against Benjamite — makes the book a chapter of covenant history and its outcome the LORD's own oath being kept.

expand to see more

Because the divine name is absent from the Hebrew of Esther, the book is commonly handled as a nationalist novella or a festival legend with no theology in it, and the repeated patronymic is passed over as courtly formality. That is to miss what the writer is doing with a phrase he repeats five times. Haman the son of Hammedatha the Agagite sets the villain in the line of Amalek, of whom the LORD swore, “the LORD hath sworn that the LORD will have war with Amalek from generation to generation” (Exo 17:16). Against him stands a man of the tribe of Benjamin descended from Kish. The reader is being told that this is not a palace intrigue but the last engagement of an ancient war.

That is also the answer to the alleged absence of God. Providence is the doctrine the book is written to display: nothing supernatural occurs, and every step — a deposed queen, a sleepless night, a forgotten record read aloud, a lot cast that fell almost a year away and gave time for a deliverance — is ordinary, and every step is governed. “The lot is cast into the lap; but the whole disposing thereof is of the LORD” (Pro 16:33) is the verse the Pur was designed to illustrate. Hammedatha's son cast lots against the covenant people and the God he did not name chose the date.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Hammedatha (H4099), Hammedatha; 'Agagi (H91), Agagite, of the house of Agag; Pur (H6332), the lot; goral (H1486), lot, portion; tsorer (H6887), adversary, enemy.

expand to see more

Hebrew Hammedatha (H4099) — Hammedatha; the father of Haman.

Hebrew 'Agagi (H91) — Agagite; descended from Agag of Amalek.

Hebrew Pur (H6332) — the Persian word for lot, whence the feast of Purim.

Hebrew goral (H1486) — lot; the Hebrew term the text glosses Pur with.

Hebrew tsorer (H6887) — adversary; ‘the Jews' enemy’.

Usage

"“Haman the son of Hammedatha the Agagite” — a patronymic repeated to name an old war."

"“The Jews' enemy” — the title the writer will not let the reader forget."

"“Had cast Pur, that is, the lot” — chance overruled by the God the book never names."
